description: Marswalk is a hyperlocal traverse-planning map for an astronaut walking on Mars. Existing tools like Mars Trek are built for regional and global views; Marswalk works at the scale of a single excursion. It adds a layer no current tool provides: a deep learning model trained on NASA JPL’s AI4Mars dataset that labels every pixel of rover imagery as soil, bedrock, sand, or big rock.
summary:
In 2009 the Spirit rover drove into soft Martian soil and never moved again. Sand and firm
soil look nearly identical in a photograph — and an astronaut in a pressurised suit, with a
restricted visor and reduced mobility, has even less chance of telling them apart.

Mars Trek and the USGS-NASA geologic maps are built for regional and global analysis. Nothing
exists at the scale of a single excursion: the ground a crew member actually crosses on one walk.

Marswalk closes that gap. A DeepLabV3+ model trained on NASA JPL's AI4Mars dataset labels every
pixel of rover imagery as soil, bedrock, sand or big rock, reaching 0.715 mean IoU and 0.913 IoU
on sand on the expert-labelled Curiosity test set — against 0.128 for an all-soil baseline. That
terrain layer is fused with MOLA/HRSC elevation for Gale Crater into a traversal cost surface,
and an A* planner routes a crew from habitat to science target around both soft ground and steep
slopes.

The result on our Gale Crater traverse: 17% extra walking distance cuts mean hazard exposure by
40%, from 0.302 to 0.180. Walk 6.8 km further, halve your exposure to the terrain that ended
Spirit's mission.
details:
MARSWALK

Intelligent Terrain-Aware Traverse Planning for Martian Missions

MARSWALK addresses this challenge by transforming Martian imagery into actionable terrain intelligence and safer exploration routes.

Using a DeepLabV3+ model trained on NASA JPL's AI4Mars dataset, MARSWALK classifies rover imagery into four terrain types: soil, bedrock, sand, and big rock, achieving 0.715 mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) on the expert-labelled Curiosity test set. The resulting terrain intelligence is combined with NASA's MOLA/HRSC elevation data to construct a terrain-aware traversal cost surface. An A* pathfinding algorithm then identifies lower-risk routes between an exploration habitat and a designated science target.

In our Gale Crater demonstration, MARSWALK achieves a 40% reduction in mean hazard exposure (0.302 to 0.180) at the cost of just 17% additional travel distance.

MARSWALK doesn't simply find the shortest path across Mars. It finds a safer one.

1. Project Details

1.1 The Problem

Martian terrain presents hazards that are difficult to identify through conventional imagery alone. Loose sand, unstable soil, steep gradients, and physical obstacles can threaten both robotic and human exploration.

Although platforms such as Mars Trek and the USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping Program provide valuable regional and global planetary mapping, they do not directly provide the hyperlocal terrain intelligence required to assess individual traverse routes.

MARSWALK bridges this gap by combining computer vision, planetary elevation data, and intelligent pathfinding into a localized terrain-aware planning system.

1.2 Our Solution

MARSWALK integrates three complementary data layers:

1. Optical Data — Curiosity Rover Imagery

  • Uses NASA Curiosity rover imagery across twelve imaging stations within the Gale Crater survey area.
  • Provides the visual input for terrain analysis and classification.

2. Terrain Intelligence — DeepLabV3+

  • Employs a DeepLabV3+ semantic segmentation architecture with a ResNet-50 encoder.
    • Soil
    • Bedrock
    • Sand
    • Big Rock
  • Achieves 0.715 mIoU on the expert-labelled test_min3 Curiosity test split.

3. Topographic Data — MOLA/HRSC DEM

  • Integrates NASA's MOLA/HRSC blended Digital Elevation Model.
  • Uses a spatial resolution of 200 metres per pixel.
  • Derives terrain slope information for the Gale Crater survey area.

Together, these layers provide the foundation for terrain-aware route planning.

1.3 Terrain-Aware Route Planning

MARSWALK converts terrain classifications and elevation-derived slope measurements into a unified traversal cost surface.

The cost function considers two primary factors:

  • Terrain Hazard: Potentially hazardous terrain, particularly sand and soil, receives higher traversal costs.
  • Slope: Steeper gradients receive disproportionately higher costs through a squared slope penalty.

Cells exceeding the 15-degree mobility threshold are marked as impassable, accounting for 11.4% of the planning grid.

An A* pathfinding algorithm then searches this cost surface to identify a lower-cost route between the exploration habitat and the designated science target.

1.4 Results and Measurable Impact

Our Gale Crater demonstration highlights the difference between conventional shortest-distance routing and terrain-aware planning.

Key Achievement: 40% Lower Mean Hazard Exposure

MARSWALK accepts a 17% increase in travel distance to achieve a 40% reduction in mean hazard exposure.

Rather than optimizing solely for distance, the system prioritizes safer terrain when selecting a route. This demonstrates how computer vision and planetary data can support more informed exploration decisions.

1.5 Model Validation

The terrain segmentation model was evaluated against NASA JPL's expert-labelled AI4Mars test_min3 dataset, which contains pixels where three rover-planning experts unanimously agreed.

The test split remained held out throughout model development.

  • Overall mIoU: 0.715
  • Soil IoU: 0.949
  • Bedrock IoU: 0.910
  • Sand IoU: 0.913
  • Big Rock IoU: 0.089
  • Pixel Accuracy: 0.961

Compared with an all-soil baseline of 0.128 mIoU, the model demonstrates substantially stronger terrain discrimination.

IoU is used as the primary evaluation metric because pixel accuracy alone can be misleading when terrain classes are heavily imbalanced.

1.6 Limitations and Scientific Considerations

MARSWALK is a research prototype and decision-support system, not an autonomous navigation solution.

Its current limitations include:

  • Illustrative Station Placement: Imaging station locations are illustrative because AI4Mars images do not contain rover coordinates.
  • Topographic Resolution: The 200 m/pixel DEM cannot capture fine-scale surface variations.
  • Class Imbalance: Big Rock represents only 0.066% of test pixels, contributing to its low precision and IoU.
  • Rover Generalisation: The model has been trained on Curiosity Navcam imagery and requires validation on other Mars missions.
  • Two-Dimensional Planning: The current planner operates on a 2D traversal cost surface rather than a complete 3D terrain model.

These limitations define the next steps toward a more operational system.

1.7 Future Potential

MARSWALK provides a foundation for expanding terrain intelligence beyond pre-planned routes.

Potential extensions include:

  • Real-Time Terrain Intelligence: Integrating live rover and spacesuit-camera imagery to update terrain classifications.
  • Astronaut Helmet HUD: Displaying terrain hazards and recommended traversal corridors directly within an astronaut's field of view.
  • Dynamic Route Replanning: Automatically recalculating recommended paths as new hazards are identified.
  • Multi-Mission Generalisation: Extending and validating the model across Perseverance, Spirit, and Opportunity imagery.
  • High-Resolution 3D Terrain Analysis: Incorporating finer topographic data to improve local hazard assessment.

Our Vision

Don't just map Mars. Understand where it is safe to walk.

MARSWALK transforms planetary imagery and topographic data into actionable terrain intelligence, helping future explorers make safer, better-informed decisions on the Martian surface.
